newsitem.title: USA: U.S. home builders say lumber pact with Canada raises costs.
newsitem.headline: U.S. home builders say lumber pact with Canada raises costs.

text.p: The National Association of Home Builders said Tuesday that the administration should scrap a U.S.-Canada lumber agreement because it has created havoc in lumber markets, caused lumber prices to soar and has increased the cost of home building.

Saying the agreement, which was finalized last spring, has added about $2,000 to the cost of building a typical single-family home in the United States, the group urged the White House to immediately renegotiate the pact.
Asked what the group would like to see in renegotiations, association President Randy Smith said, "We think the whole deal should be ripped up. We think it's inappropriate."
Officials at the U.S. Trade Representative's Office were quick to respond and rejected the request.
"We stand by our agreement and we will make no changes," said spokeswoman Kirsten Powers. The Trade Representative's Office led the negotiations for Washington in coming up with the agreement.

The controversial agreement, which was crafted after years of squabbling between the U.S. and Canadian lumber industries, allows 14.7 billion board feet of lumber to be shipped free into the United States from the Canadian provinces of British Columbia, Quebec, Ontario and Alberta.
Shipments above that level are slapped with import tariffs of $50 and $100 per thousand board feet.
U.S. lumber producers have long charged that Canada subsidizes its lumber industry, allowing Canadian growers to sell their lumber in American markets at cheap prices.
As much as one-third of the lumber used in the United States comes from Canada, and one-half of the framing lumber used in building U.S. homes is imported from Canada.
Lumber costs account for 8 percent to 9 percent of the total price of a house, according to statistics from the home builders association.

Lumber prices have been gyrating wildly since the signing of the agreement and are up some 30 percent from April levels. Prices peaked in early November when Canada first announced the individual quotas being assigned to lumber exporters, and rumors swirled that exports would be stopped or cut sharply.

Since then, lumber prices have backed off, partly in response to continued shipments from Canada, but largely due to recent reports that home building is slowing because of a more stagnant economy and more level demand.
Supporters of the agreement said lumber prices will continue to level out, and that the agreement has not been the sole cause of lumber's price jump.

"Lumber prices were going to go up anyway ... the home builders are taking a very isolated sector," said John Rogosta, spokesman for the Coalition for Fair Lumber Imports, the group that spearheaded the push to limit Canadian lumber shipments into the United States.
